findings.title: `order()` added as abstract method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: `int order();` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` interface without a `default` implementation. `CryptoProvider` is an SPI loaded via `ServiceLoader`, so any implementation outside this repository (adapters, downstream/3rd-party crypto providers, test doubles) will fail to compile and will throw `AbstractMethodError` at runtime when `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` sorts providers. Giving the method a sensible `default` (e.g. `return 100;` or `0`) would keep the SPI backward compatible while still allowing providers to override the preference.

findings.title: Equal-order providers are now silently resolved instead of failing fast (FIPS vs non-FIPS)
findings.body: The previous code threw `IllegalStateException` when more than one `CryptoProvider` was found, which protected against a misconfigured classpath. Now the list is sorted by `order()` and the first entry is used unconditionally. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return `order() == 200`, so if e.g. both the default (non-FIPS BouncyCastle) and the FIPS provider jars end up on the classpath, the selection depends on undefined `ServiceLoader` iteration order and the server may silently start with the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider in a deployment that must be FIPS-compliant, with only a debug-level log line. Either keep failing on an order tie, or give the server-side providers distinct orders and log at WARN when multiple providers of the same order are present.

findings.title: Dynamic string passed as format to logger.debugf
findings.body: `logger.debugf(builder.toString())` passes a dynamically built message as the format string of a formatting logger method (with no arguments). Any `%` character appearing in a provider class name would cause an `UnknownFormatConversionException`/`MissingFormatArgumentException` from the logging call. Use `logger.debug(builder.toString())` or `logger.debugf("%s", builder)` instead.

findings.title: concatenatedRSToASN1DER does not validate the input signature length
findings.body: `System.arraycopy(signature, 0, r, 1, len)` / `System.arraycopy(signature, len, s, 1, len)` assume `signature.length == signLength`. For an attacker-supplied token whose signature part is shorter (or where the wrong algorithm length is used), this throws an unchecked `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` out of a method declared to throw `IOException`, so callers doing signature verification will see an unexpected runtime failure instead of a clean "invalid signature" error. The BouncyCastle-based implementations validate the length and throw `IOException`; the same check should be added here.

findings.title: Indefinite-length encoding (-1) leads to NegativeArraySizeException instead of IOException
findings.body: `readLength()` returns `-1` for the indefinite-length form (0x80), but callers do not handle it: `readInteger()` passes it directly to `read(length)`, which does `new byte[-1]` and throws an unchecked `NegativeArraySizeException`. Since this decoder parses attacker-controlled DER signature bytes, malformed input escapes as an unchecked exception rather than the declared `IOException` (and in `readSequence()` an indefinite length silently yields an empty list). DER does not allow indefinite lengths at all here, so `readLength()` should reject 0x80 with an `IOException`, or every caller must check for `-1`.

findings.title: Dead encoder calls in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: Lines 114-115 create two `ASN1Encoder` instances, write `rBigInteger`/`sBigInteger` into them and discard the results; the actual DER sequence is built from freshly created encoders on lines 117-121. These two statements have no effect and only allocate; they should be removed to avoid suggesting the encoders are stateful/shared.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default keystore's JDK provider
findings.body: `getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, i.e. typically `SUN`, not a BouncyCastle provider. `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER` is derived from this provider's name and is used elsewhere as the explicit provider argument for `Signature.getInstance(alg, PROVIDER)`, `KeyFactory.getInstance(alg, PROVIDER)` etc. If any code reached with this crypto provider active uses `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER`, it will request algorithms from a provider that does not implement them and fail with `NoSuchAlgorithmException`. Returning `null` (as `WildFlyElytronProvider` does) or throwing `UnsupportedOperationException` would make the unsupported nature explicit.

findings.title: ECDSA conversion test uses one default curve and never verifies the produced DER
findings.body: The key pair is generated once with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` default parameters (P-256), so the ES384 and ES512 cases are exercised with 32-byte r/s values zero-padded to 48/66 bytes; the real cases (secp384r1/secp521r1 signatures, including the 521-bit odd byte length that is the usual source of off-by-one bugs) are never covered. In addition the test only asserts a round-trip of the new implementation against itself (`rsConcat` vs `rsConcat2`), so a systematic encoding error would pass. The test should generate a key per curve (`ECGenParameterSpec` secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) and verify the DER output with `Signature.verify()` (and/or compare with the BouncyCastle-based provider output).
